taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes T. hammondii, T. gigas and T. atratus (with hydrophilus and aquaticus) were formerly included in T. couchii; CWHR places Thamnophis in Natricidae while NatureServe uses Colubridae.
fieldMarks: Medium-sized, slender, highly aquatic garter snake with a somewhat pointed head.
Found in or right beside water, basking in streamside vegetation and fleeing into water when disturbed.
behavior: Active diurnal snake: low-elevation animals can be active about 10 months a year, high-elevation ones less than 4 months.
Forages in and along water: larval and newly transformed amphibians in ephemeral water; fish (trout, Sacramento suckers, mosquitofish) in permanent streams.
Retreats at night to holes, crevices and surface objects and rapidly to water when disturbed; young are born July-September in secluded sites such as under bark.
habitat: Pools of permanent or seasonal streams (often rocky), meadow ponds, lakes, reservoirs and riparian zones, in oak woodland, chaparral, montane conifer forest, or pine-juniper-sagebrush east of the Sierra crest.
range: Sierra Nevada of California from the Pit and Sacramento rivers south to the Tehachapi Mountains, east along major rivers to the Owens Valley and west-central Nevada, about 90-2,440 m. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Aquatic gartersnake (Thamnophis atratus)
lookalikes.howToTell: Distinguished mainly by range; aquatic gartersnake occupies the Coast Ranges west of the Central Valley.

lookalikes.name: Terrestrial gartersnake (Thamnophis elegans)
lookalikes.howToTell: Sierra gartersnake is much more tightly tied to water; terrestrial gartersnake also ranges into drier habitats.
